## Introduction 

Press any C on a piano, then count the keys before you reach the next one. Twelve notes: seven white keys, five black. I've played this layout for decades, and only recently did it strike me as strange. Why twelve? Why not ten, fifteen or even fifty-three *(wink)*?

The easy answer is convenience. A few more notes per octave would add around twenty keys *(the horror)*. But convenience explains why we don't have fifty-three notes per octave; but not why don't we do ten, or seven, which would be even easier. And tuning systems with 19, 24, even 31 notes per octave exist, just glance at Wikipedia [@wikivarieties] on this topic. So, again: why twelve?

My suspicion is that the magic number comes from something deeper: hidden within the arithmetic of musical intervals. This article document my journey of discovering this truth. Beware: there will be mathematics.

## The Physics of Pitches

We must first start by introducing the fundamental unit of music - a note. Physically, a note is just air pressure wobbling back and forth. What sets apart notes are its pitches, measured in **frequency**.

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
### What are frequencies?
Frequency is how many times something repeats each second. A vibrating string swings back and forth, and one full back-and-forth is a *cycle*. The number of cycles per second is measured in *hertz* (Hz). A 3 Hz wave completes 3 cycles every second, and a 6 Hz wave completes 6, so it repeats twice as fast.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Two waves over one second. The lower one has twice the frequency."
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
t = np.linspace(0, 1, 1000)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 2.8), sharex=True)
for ax, f in zip(axes, [3, 6]):
    ax.plot(t, np.sin(2 * np.pi * f * t))
    ax.set_ylabel(f"{f} Hz")
    ax.set_yticks([])
axes[-1].set_xlabel("Time (s)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

For sound, frequency is pitch: more cycles per second sounds higher. The A string's 110 Hz means it swings back and forth 110 times every second.
:::

But a note is never one frequency. If you pluck the open A string on a guitar, a tuner will tell you it's 110 Hz. But run the same sound through a spectrum analyzer, and odds are you will be surprised. It turns out that there are multiple frequencies in a note, not just 110 Hz, but 220, 330 Hz, and so on. The lowest of these, 110 Hz, is the *fundamental*, and it sets the pitch you hear. The rest, at whole-number multiples of it, are the *harmonics*, or overtones.


```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
from scipy import signal
from IPython.display import Audio, display
import soundfile as sf

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
integrate = getattr(np, "trapezoid", None) or np.trapz

L = 1.0        # string length
f1 = 110.0     # open A string, in Hz
fs = 44100     # audio sample rate
```

Here is a recording of an open A string, plucked three times. Its fundamental $f_0$ is 110 Hz, so we expect energy at $f_0, 2f_0, 3f_0, 4f_0, \ldots$, or at 110, 220, 330, 440 Hz and so on respectively.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
audio_path = "record.mp3"
samples, record_fs = sf.read(audio_path, always_2d=False)
if samples.ndim > 1:
    samples = samples.mean(axis=1)  # collapse stereo to mono for analysis

display(Audio(audio_path))
```

A spectrogram shows which frequencies are present at each moment, and brighter indicates higher energy. The dashed lines mark where the theoretical harmonics should be:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Spectrogram of the recorded A string. Dashed lines mark the fundamental $f_0$ and harmonics $f_n = n f_0$."
freqs, t, Sxx = signal.spectrogram(samples, fs=record_fs, nperseg=4096, noverlap=3072, window="hann")
Sxx_db = 10 * np.log10(Sxx + 1e-12)
f0 = 110

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
mesh = ax.pcolormesh(
    t, freqs, Sxx_db, shading="gouraud", cmap="magma",
    vmin=np.percentile(Sxx_db, 25), vmax=Sxx_db.max(),
)

ax.set_ylim(0, 4000)
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Frequency (Hz)")
fig.colorbar(mesh, ax=ax, label="Energy (dB)")

for n in range(1, int(4000 / f0) + 1):
    ax.axhline(n * f0, color="white", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.6, alpha=0.5)
    ax.text(t[-1], n * f0, f"  {n}×f0", color="white", va="center", fontsize=7)

plt.show()
```

Two things stand out:

1. **The bands sit on the dashed lines.** Energy is concentrated at whole-number multiples of 110 Hz, just as predicted.

   :::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
   ### **Real strings are not perfectly elastic!**
   Real harmonics roughly follow $f_n \approx n \cdot f_0 \cdot \sqrt{1 + B n^2}$, where $B$ is the inharmonicity coefficient. Dashed lines may not be perfectly alligned with the peaks.
   :::

2. **Higher harmonics are weaker and shorter-lived.** Most of the energy sits below about 1000 Hz, and the upper bands fade within a second or so while the low ones ring on.

For why harmonics exist, see my writing on the physics of harmonics in [On Harmonics](../harmonics/index.qmd).
